```{r}
#| label: setup

library(bmm)
library(brms)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)
source(here::here("_common.R"))
dat_simple <- read.csv(here::here("data", "m3_simple_span.csv"))
dat_simple$ss_fac <- factor(dat_simple$ss_fac, levels = c(2, 4, 6, 8))
fit_simple <- readRDS(here::here("models", "m3_simple.rds"))
```

Scan the QR code to open the workshop materials.

Open `examples/02_m3.qmd` for data, code, pre-fitted models, and checks.

In this session, we will:

- Identify the **activation sources** supporting each response.
- Translate activation into choice probabilities using **softmax and option counts**.
- Estimate **item and binding memory** with bmm.
- Extend the model to examine **distractor filtering**.

## Baseline and memory activation {#each-option-receives-activation auto-animate=true}

```{=html}
<svg data-id="m3-activation-plot" viewBox="0 0 1000 440" width="100%" height="440" role="img" aria-labelledby="m3-activation-title m3-activation-desc">
  <title id="m3-activation-title">Baseline and memory activation for old and new objects</title>
  <desc id="m3-activation-desc">Initially only axes and options are visible. The first click shows baseline b for both options; the second adds memory activation a above the old object's baseline; the new object remains at b. Heights are illustrative.</desc>
  <line x1="150" y1="320" x2="880" y2="320" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>

```

::: {.notes}
Start with axes and options only. The first click shows both grey baseline
bars and b labels; the second adds the blue memory segment only to old. Bar heights are schematic, not parameter
estimates. Activation supports a choice; a is not a storage probability.
:::

## Choice probabilities: Luce’s choice rule {#simple-choice-rule auto-animate=true}

:::: {.columns .m3-choice-layout}

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{=html}
<svg data-id="m3-activation-plot" viewBox="0 0 1000 440" width="100%" height="440" role="img" aria-labelledby="m3-simple-activation-title m3-simple-activation-desc">
  <title id="m3-simple-activation-title">Baseline and memory activation for old and new objects</title>
  <desc id="m3-simple-activation-desc">Old has baseline b plus memory activation a; new has baseline b. Bar heights are illustrative.</desc>
  <line x1="150" y1="320" x2="880" y2="320" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="150" y1="320" x2="150" y2="45" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="95" y="185" transform="rotate(-90 95 185)" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Activation</text>
  <rect x="300" y="270" width="130" height="50" fill="#7f7f7f"/>
  <rect x="650" y="270" width="130" height="50" fill="#7f7f7f"/>
  <g font-size="34" fill="white" text-anchor="middle" font-style="italic">
    <text x="365" y="307">b</text><text x="715" y="307">b</text>
  </g>
  <g >
    <rect x="300" y="130" width="130" height="140" fill="#0028a5"/>
    <text x="365" y="212" font-size="34" text-anchor="middle" font-style="italic" fill="white">a</text>
  </g>
  <g text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="365" y="375" font-size="42">🪑</text><text x="715" y="375" font-size="42">🚲</text>
    <text x="365" y="420" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Old object</text><text x="715" y="420" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">New object</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

:::

::: {.column .m3-choice-formulas width="55%"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}

$$
P(\mathrm{old})=
\frac{b+a}{(b+a)+b}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

$$
P(\mathrm{new})=
\frac{b}{(b+a)+b}
$$

:::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Reference: Oberauer & Lewandowsky (2019), Eq. 2, applied to this teaching
recognition example. Normalize the activation values directly: old receives
b+a, new receives b. Point to each contribution in the shared denominator.
This rule uses nonnegative activation values with a positive total; a fixed
positive baseline sets their scale. The original paper fixed b at 0.1.
:::

## Choice probabilities: Softmax {#softmax-choice-rule auto-animate=true}

:::: {.columns .m3-choice-layout}

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{=html}
<svg data-id="m3-activation-plot" viewBox="0 0 1000 440" width="100%" height="440" role="img" aria-labelledby="m3-softmax-activation-title m3-softmax-activation-desc">
  <title id="m3-softmax-activation-title">Baseline and memory activation for old and new objects</title>
  <desc id="m3-softmax-activation-desc">Old has baseline b plus memory activation a; new has baseline b. Bar heights are illustrative.</desc>
  <line x1="150" y1="320" x2="880" y2="320" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="150" y1="320" x2="150" y2="45" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="95" y="185" transform="rotate(-90 95 185)" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Activation</text>
  <rect x="300" y="270" width="130" height="50" fill="#7f7f7f"/>
  <rect x="650" y="270" width="130" height="50" fill="#7f7f7f"/>
  <g font-size="34" fill="white" text-anchor="middle" font-style="italic">
    <text x="365" y="307">b</text><text x="715" y="307">b</text>
  </g>
  <g >
    <rect x="300" y="130" width="130" height="140" fill="#0028a5"/>
    <text x="365" y="212" font-size="34" text-anchor="middle" font-style="italic" fill="white">a</text>
  </g>
  <g text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="365" y="375" font-size="42">🪑</text><text x="715" y="375" font-size="42">🚲</text>
    <text x="365" y="420" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Old object</text><text x="715" y="420" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">New object</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

:::

::: {.column .m3-choice-formulas width="55%"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}

$$
P(\mathrm{old})=
\frac{\exp(b+a)}{\exp(b+a)+\exp(b)}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

$$
P(\mathrm{new})=
\frac{\exp(b)}{\exp(b+a)+\exp(b)}
$$

:::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Choice-rule reference: Oberauer (2023), Eq. 4.
Now transform the same activations with exp before normalizing. These are
alternative choice rules with different parameter scales, not equivalent
rewritings of one model. Use softmax in all subsequent examples.
Point from each numerator to the corresponding image on the preceding slide.
Both options compete in the same choice and share a denominator. Their
probabilities sum to one. A common b cancels from softmax; keep it visible
to explain activation sources rather than estimating it independently.
:::

## Memory activation and choice probabilities {#stronger-item-memory-favors-the-old-image .m3-figure}

```{r}
#| label: recognition-demo
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Illustrative softmax probabilities: old and new are equally likely when memory activation is zero; greater memory activation favors old."
recognition_demo <- expand_grid(a = c(0, 1, 2), option = c("Old", "New")) |>
  mutate(b = 1, activation = b + if_else(option == "Old", a, 0),
         weight = exp(activation)) |>
  mutate(probability = weight / sum(weight), .by = a)
recognition_demo |>
  ggplot(aes(option, probability, fill = option)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", probability)), vjust = -0.4, size = 6) +
  facet_wrap(~a, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Old", "New")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(New = wk_colors[["grey"]], Old = wk_colors[["blue"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Choice probability") + theme_workshop() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 20))
```

```{=html}
<div class="m3-task">
  <div class="m3-screen m3-stage m3-spatial" aria-label="Sequential presentation: apple at left, chair at center, car at right.">
    <span class="m3-stim m3-left fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="0" role="img" aria-label="apple at left">🍎</span>
```

The key change is the instruction to remember image–location associations.

logic. These intervals are for the teaching demonstration.

## Item and binding activation {#three-options-reveal-two-memory-sources .m3-binding-slide auto-animate=true}

:::: {.m3-binding-layout}

::: {.m3-binding-diagram}

```{=html}
<svg data-id="m3-binding-plot" viewBox="0 -70 1000 550" width="100%" height="440" role="img" aria-labelledby="binding-title binding-desc">
  <title id="binding-title">Item and binding activation</title>
  <desc id="binding-desc">All three options receive baseline b. Memory activation a is added to correct and other. Binding activation c is added only to correct. Heights are illustrative.</desc>
  <line x1="150" y1="340" x2="920" y2="340" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="150" y1="340" x2="150" y2="-60" stroke="#4a5568" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="95" y="185" transform="rotate(-90 95 185)" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Activation</text>
  <g>
  <g fill="#7f7f7f">
    <rect data-fragment-index="0" class="fragment m3-grow-bar" x="245" y="290" width="110" height="50"/>
    <rect data-fragment-index="0" class="fragment m3-grow-bar" x="490" y="290" width="110" height="50"/>
    <rect data-fragment-index="0" class="fragment m3-grow-bar" x="735" y="290" width="110" height="50"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="white" font-size="34" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle">
    <text data-fragment-index="0" class="fragment fade-in" x="300" y="327">b</text><text data-fragment-index="0" class="fragment fade-in" x="545" y="327">b</text><text data-fragment-index="0" class="fragment fade-in" x="790" y="327">b</text>
  </g>
  </g>
  <g>
    <rect data-fragment-index="1" class="fragment m3-grow-bar" x="245" y="150" width="110" height="140" fill="#0028a5"/>
    <rect data-fragment-index="1" class="fragment m3-grow-bar" x="490" y="150" width="110" height="140" fill="#0028a5"/>
    <g fill="white" font-size="34" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle">
      <text data-fragment-index="1" class="fragment fade-in" x="300" y="232">a</text><text data-fragment-index="1" class="fragment fade-in" x="545" y="232">a</text>
    </g>
  </g>
  <g>
    <rect data-fragment-index="2" class="fragment m3-grow-bar" x="245" y="-40" width="110" height="190" fill="#dc6800"/>
    <text data-fragment-index="2" class="fragment fade-in" x="300" y="67" font-size="34" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">c</text>
  </g>
  <g text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="300" y="397" font-size="42">🪑</text><text x="545" y="397" font-size="42">🍎</text><text x="790" y="397" font-size="42">🚲</text>
    <text x="300" y="442" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Correct</text><text x="545" y="442" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">Others</text><text x="790" y="442" font-size="28" fill="#4a5568">New</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

:::

::: {.m3-binding-formula .fragment fragment-index=3}

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\mathrm{correct}) &= b + a + c \\
A(\mathrm{other}) &= b + a \\
A(\mathrm{new}) &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Start with axes and options only. The first click shows the three grey
baseline bars and b labels; the second adds item activation a to both studied
images; the third adds orange binding c only
to the cued image. Do not add total labels above the bars. The sources follow
Oberauer & Lewandowsky (2019), Eq. 1; this task is a teaching example.

:::

## Memory activation and choice probabilities {#what-does-binding-add .m3-figure}

```{r}
#| label: binding-demo
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Illustrative predictions holding item activation fixed: correct and other are equally likely without binding; adding binding increases correct choices."
binding_demo <- expand_grid(c = c(0, 1, 2), option = c("Correct", "Others", "New")) |>
  mutate(option = factor(option, levels = c("Correct", "Others", "New")),
         b = 1, a = 1,
         activation = b + if_else(option == "New", 0, a) + if_else(option == "Correct", c, 0),
         weight = exp(activation)) |>
  mutate(probability = weight / sum(weight), .by = c)
binding_demo |>
  ggplot(aes(option, probability, fill = option)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~c, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(wk_colors[c("blue", "orange", "grey")]), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Choice probability") + theme_workshop() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 20))
```

::: {.notes}
These are illustrative predictions with fixed a. Without binding, correct
and other have equal activation; increasing c favors correct.
:::

Estimating item and binding memory with bmm.

## Example of a simple-span task {#simple-span .m3-timed data-autoslide="900" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide}

## Specifying the simple-span model {#specify-categories-and-their-option-counts .smaller .m3-model-slide}
[[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track}

::::: {.m3-model-content}

```{r}
#| label: model-simple
#| code-line-numbers: "1-7|2|3|4|5|6"
model_simple <- m3(
  resp_cats = c("corr", "other", "npl"),
  num_options = c("n_corr", "n_other", "n_npl"),
  version = "ss",
  choice_rule = "softmax",
  links = list(a = "identity", c = "identity")
)
```

```{=html}
<script>
document.querySelector('#specify-categories-and-their-option-counts .sourceCode code').setAttribute('data-fragment-index', '0');
</script>
```

:::: {.m3-model-explanations}

::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=0}
`resp_cats`: observed response counts for Correct, Others, and NPL.
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=1}
`num_options`: available options in the same category order.
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=2}
`version`: `"ss"` = simple span · `"cs"` = complex span · `"custom"` = custom model.

:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=3}
`choice_rule`: `"simple"` = Luce’s choice rule · `"softmax"` = exponential choice weights.

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
::::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=7}
`links`: map regression predictors to parameter values.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="33%" fragment-index=4}

### identity

```{r}
#| label: link-identity
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Identity inverse link: parameter value equals the regression predictor, including negative values."
link_predictors <- tibble(eta = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 201))
ggplot(link_predictors, aes(eta, eta)) +
  geom_line(color = wk_colors[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Link scale", y = "Original scale") + theme_workshop()
```

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="33%" fragment-index=5}

### log

```{r}
#| label: link-log
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log inverse link: exponentiating the regression predictor produces positive parameter values."
ggplot(link_predictors, aes(eta, exp(eta))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = wk_colors[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = wk_colors[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 21)) +
  labs(x = "Link scale", y = "Original scale") + theme_workshop()
```

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="33%" fragment-index=6}

### logit

```{r}
#| label: link-logit
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Logit inverse link: a logistic curve maps the regression predictor to parameter values between zero and one."
ggplot(link_predictors, aes(eta, plogis(eta))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), color = wk_colors[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = wk_colors[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Link scale", y = "Original scale") + theme_workshop()
```

:::
::::
:::::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=7}

:::: {.columns .m3-choice-comparison}
::: {.column .m3-choice-panel width="100%"}

### simple

::: {.m3-choice-equation}

$$
P(k)=\frac{n_k A_k}{\sum_j n_j A_j}
$$

```{=html}
<div class="m3-formula-callout fragment" data-fragment-index="8" role="note">
  <svg aria-hidden="true"><path></path></svg>
  <div class="m3-callout-label"><span class="m3-callout-emphasis">Cannot</span> be negative</div>
</div>
```

:::

:::
::: {.column .m3-choice-panel width="100%"}

### softmax

::: {.m3-choice-equation}

$$
P(k)=\frac{n_k\exp(A_k)}{\sum_j n_j\exp(A_j)}
$$

```{=html}
<div class="m3-formula-callout fragment" data-fragment-index="8" role="note">
  <svg aria-hidden="true"><path></path></svg>
  <div class="m3-callout-label">Can be negative</div>
</div>
```

:::

:::
::::

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.notes}
Initially show the complete code without dimmed lines or explanations.
Each click highlights the next parameter and shows its explanation together:
resp_cats, num_options, version, then choice_rule. Valid options were checked against
the installed bmm 1.3.1 m3 constructor. The native Quarto line-highlight
plugin uses the code's initial fragment index to align its cloned steps.
The conceptual b remains in teaching formulas. The implementation fixes the
common baseline for identification; it cancels from softmax. Only a and c
need regression formulas. Do not present b as a third estimable parameter.
:::

## Specifying parameter formulas {#specify-how-do-a-and-c-vary .smaller}
[[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track}

```{r}
#| label: formula-simple
#| code-line-numbers: true
formula_simple <- bmf(
  c ~ 0 + ss_fac + (0 + ss_fac | id),
  a ~ 0 + ss_fac + (0 + ss_fac | id)
)
```

::: {.incremental}
- `0 + ss_fac`: a separate mean for each **set size**.
- `(0 + ss_fac | id)`: correlated participant deviations at each set size.
:::

::: {.notes}
ss_fac treats set size as categorical. Both fixed and participant effects
use one coefficient per set size, without a separate intercept. The fit uses
only open-set data. The vertical bar retains correlations between each
participant's deviations at different set sizes.
:::

## Setting priors: simple {#setting-priors-simple .smaller}
[[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track}

**Log link:** priors on the log-activation scale.

```{r}
#| eval: false
coefs <- paste0("ss_fac", c(2, 4, 6, 8))
priors_simple_rule <- c(
  set_prior("normal(1, 0.5)", nlpar = "a", coef = coefs),
  set_prior("normal(1.5, 0.5)", nlpar = "c", coef = coefs)
)
```

These priors apply to the set-size means of log activation.
The log link keeps $a$ and $c$ positive.

```{r}
#| label: prior-simple-density
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Priors for a and c: normal densities on the link scale and their lognormal densities on the original scale, shown in blue and orange."
prior_simple_density <- bind_rows(
  expand_grid(parameter = c("a", "c"), value = seq(-1, 3.5, length.out = 401)) |>
    mutate(scale = "Link scale",
           density = dnorm(value, mean = if_else(parameter == "a", 1, 1.5), sd = 0.5)),
  expand_grid(parameter = c("a", "c"), value = seq(0, qlnorm(0.995, 1.5, 0.5), length.out = 401)) |>
    mutate(scale = "Original scale",
           density = dlnorm(value, meanlog = if_else(parameter == "a", 1, 1.5), sdlog = 0.5))
) |>
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Link scale", "Original scale")))
ggplot(prior_simple_density, aes(value, density, color = parameter, linetype = parameter)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~scale, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(a = wk_colors[["blue"]], c = wk_colors[["orange"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(a = "solid", c = "dashed")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_workshop() + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## Setting priors: softmax {#setting-priors-softmax .smaller}
[[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track}

**Identity link:** priors on the activation scale.

```{r}
#| eval: false
coefs <- paste0("ss_fac", c(2, 4, 6, 8))
priors_softmax <- c(
  set_prior("normal(3, 1)", nlpar = "a", coef = coefs),
  set_prior("normal(3, 1)", nlpar = "c", coef = coefs)
)
```

These priors apply to the set-size means of activation.
They are the priors used in this workshop fit.

```{r}
#| label: prior-softmax-density
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Priors for a and c are both Normal(3, 1); link-scale and original-scale densities are identical under the identity link. The blue solid and orange dashed curves coincide."
prior_softmax_density <- expand_grid(
  parameter = c("a", "c"), scale = c("Link scale", "Original scale"),
  value = seq(-1, 7, length.out = 401)
) |>
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Link scale", "Original scale")),
         density = dnorm(value, mean = 3, sd = 1))
ggplot(prior_softmax_density, aes(value, density, color = parameter, linetype = parameter)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~scale, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(a = wk_colors[["blue"]], c = wk_colors[["orange"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(a = "solid", c = "dashed")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_workshop() + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## Fitting M3 with bmm {#fit-once-load-the-result-for-the-workshop .smaller .m3-model-slide}
[specify · [fit]{.on} · evaluate]{.track}

::::: {.m3-model-content}

```{r}
#| label: fit-simple-settings
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: true
fit_simple <- bmm(
  formula = formula_simple,
  model = model_simple,
  data = dat_simple,
  prior = priors_softmax,
  chains = 4, cores = 4,
  iter = 5000, warmup = 2000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  sample_prior = "yes",
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  seed = 2026
)
```

The sampling arguments work the same way as in the SDT model.

:::::

## Model fit: Observed and predicted responses {#evaluate-does-m3-reproduce-the-responses .smaller .m3-figure}
[specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track}

`posterior_epred(fit_simple)` predicts counts in **all three categories**.

```{r}
#| label: predictive-check
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Observed and predicted open-set response proportions, with participant-level standard errors, across three categories."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("data", "figures", "m3_simple_predictive.png"))
```

::: {.notes}
Compare observed and predicted means, including both error categories.
Error bars are ±1 participant-level SE, not posterior predictive intervals.
Close mean curves do not establish that every aspect of fit is adequate.
:::

## Parameter estimates: Item and binding memory {#interpret-item-memory-and-binding-memory .smaller .m3-figure}
[specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track}

```{r}
#| label: posterior-plot
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Open-set item and binding memory medians and 95 percent credible intervals across set sizes, in blue and orange facets on a 0 to 6 activation scale."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("data", "figures", "m3_simple_parameters.png"))
```

::: {.small}
Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals; parameters are on the activation scale.
:::

::: {.notes}
Binding estimates have lower posterior medians at larger set sizes in the open set.
Describe item-memory patterns separately rather than treating accuracy as a
single memory parameter. These are model-based estimates under the chosen
activation and choice rules.
:::

## Extending M3 to complex span {.section-divider}

How does M3 account for distractor activation?

```{=html}
    </div>
```

::: {.notes}
Simplified complex-span demonstration based on Li, Frischkorn, and Oberauer
(2026), Experiment 1.
Press next to begin. The published arrow cue is replaced by a circular
outline here as a simplified teaching display. The white ring appears with the pair and selects the memorandum during
processing. It has a white outline and no fill.
Both objects share a context color; processing requires selecting the larger
object in real life. The target is designated before the size judgment.
This example and the fitted application both use the pre-cue condition.

## Example of a complex-span task {#targets-and-distractors .m3-timed data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="m3-task"><div class="m3-screen m3-complex-screen m3-stage" aria-label="Three ring-cued pairs sharing green, purple, and orange context colors.">
<div class="m3-complex-state fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1" data-autoslide="0"><p class="m3-complex-prompt">Which object is larger?</p><button class="m3-complex-object m3-target-ring" aria-label="avocado" data-processing-choice="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 768 768" aria-hidden="true"><image href="images/complex-span/image1-green.svg" width="768" height="768"/></svg></button><button class="m3-complex-object" aria-label="crocodile" data-processing-choice="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 768 768" aria-hidden="true"><image href="images/complex-span/image5-green.svg" width="768" height="768"/></svg><img class="m3-demo-cursor fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0" src="images/standard-cursor.svg" alt="Mouse pointer on the correct size-judgment choice"></button></div>
<div class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><div class="m3-complex-state fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="3" data-autoslide="0"><p class="m3-complex-prompt">Which object is larger?</p><button class="m3-complex-object" aria-label="banana" data-processing-choice="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 768 768" aria-hidden="true"><image href="images/complex-span/image2-purple.svg" width="768" height="768"/></svg></button><button class="m3-complex-object m3-target-ring" aria-label="flamingo" data-processing-choice="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 768 768" aria-hidden="true"><image href="images/complex-span/image8-purple.svg" width="768" height="768"/></svg><img class="m3-demo-cursor fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2" src="images/standard-cursor.svg" alt="Mouse pointer on the correct size-judgment choice"></button></div></div>
<div class="m3-complex-state fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3" data-autoslide="0"><p class="m3-complex-prompt">Which object is larger?</p><button class="m3-complex-object" aria-label="octopus" data-processing-choice="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 768 768" aria-hidden="true"><image href="images/complex-span/image24-orange.svg" width="768" height="768"/></svg><img class="m3-demo-cursor fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="4" src="images/standard-cursor.svg" alt="Mouse pointer on the correct size-judgment choice"></button><button class="m3-complex-object m3-target-ring" aria-label="croissant" data-processing-choice="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 768 768" aria-hidden="true"><image href="images/complex-span/image4-orange.svg" width="768" height="768"/></svg></button></div>
</div></div>
<script>
document.querySelectorAll('#targets-and-distractors [data-processing-choice]').forEach(button => {
  button.addEventListener('click', event => {
    event.stopPropagation();
    Reveal.next();
  });
});
</script>
```

::: {.notes}
This simplified display is presenter-paced. The white ring and the two
objects appear simultaneously. Press next (or click an object) to show the
following pair directly. After the last pair, press next to open the test.
No blank stages or automatic timers remain.
The original experiment allowed up to 2500 ms for processing and a
1500-ms post-processing interval; this demonstration does not reproduce
those durations, record responses, or score choices. Each target/distractor pair differs by
at least two levels in the authors' size ratings: image5/image1 = 4/2,
image8/image2 = 4/2, and image24/image4 = 6/2.
The targets are avocado, flamingo, croissant. The first and third targets
are the smaller objects; the second is the larger object. The size-judgment
question still asks for the larger object in every pair. Three context colors follow the
published hue spacing. Original silhouettes are from the public OSF materials.
The stimuli are a teaching selection, not the particular trial in Figure 1.
:::

```{=html}
</div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
The color cue probes flamingo, not a spatial location or pair index. The
12 choices are 1 correct, 1 same-color distractor, 2 other targets,
2 other distractors, and 6 NPLs. The response categories are introduced on the following slide after the
audience has selected a response. In the experiment each of the three colors was
probed in randomized order with a 10-second response deadline; the slide
shows one test and remains until the presenter advances. White silhouettes,
context cue and two simultaneous objects match the published design; this
is a reconstruction using original assets, not an archived screenshot.
Source: Li et al. (2026), Experiment 1, Figure 1; doi:10.1037/xlm0001585.
:::

::: {.m3-binding-formula .m3-category-activations .fragment fragment-index=4}

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\mathrm{correct}) &= b + a + c \\
A(\mathrm{paired\ distractor}) &= b + f a + f c \\
A(\mathrm{other\ targets}) &= b + a \\
A(\mathrm{other\ distractors}) &= b + f a \\
A(\mathrm{NPL}) &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The bars show one representative option per category. Start with axes and
options only. First show baseline b, then item activation a, then binding activation c
on three separate clicks. The fourth click illustrates filtering with f=0.5. Baseline is unchanged. Both distractor
item and binding contributions are retained at 50% in the standard
cs model. Original bar heights are preserved: removed portions are outlined
with dashed borders and 20% fill opacity; solid portions show fa and fc.
Filtering reduces each solid segment from its top down over 0.5 seconds,
while the removed portion expands down from its original top.
This shared multiplier is a model assumption, not a universal
claim about filtering. f=0 leaves baseline alone. Bar heights and f=0.5
are teaching values, not fitted results. A larger c in the illustration is
not an invariant property. See tutorial pp. 20–22 for the activation formulas.
Show the activation decomposition for each response category on the final
click. Each formula is activation per option, not a category probability.
The same f scales item and binding activation for distractors in the standard
bmm complex-span model.
:::

## Specifying the complex-span model {#extend-the-model-keep-the-workflow .smaller}
[[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track}

```{r}
#| eval: false
model_complex <- m3(
  resp_cats = c("corr", "distc", "other", "disto", "npl"),
  num_options = c("n_corr", "n_distc", "n_other", "n_disto", "n_npl"),
  version = "cs", choice_rule = "softmax"
)

formula_complex <- bmf(
  c ~ 1 + (1 | participant),
  a ~ 1 + (1 | participant),
  f ~ 1 + (1 | participant)
)
```

## Model fit: Observed and predicted responses {#evaluate-complex-span-fit .smaller .m3-figure}
[specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track}

```{r}
#| label: complex-predictive-check
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Observed and predicted pre-cue response proportions in Correct and Errors facets. Errors contains four response categories; the legend is on the right."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("data", "figures", "m3_complex_predictive.png"))
```

::: {.notes}
Error bars are ±1 participant-level SE. Correct uses a 0.5–0.9 scale;
Errors uses 0–0.20. The model underpredicts other-distractor responses.
Acknowledge this discrepancy before interpreting the filtering parameter.
:::

## Parameter estimates: Item, binding, and filtering {#interpret-the-extension-alongside-model-fit .smaller .m3-figure}
[specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track}

```{r}
#| label: complex-parameter-plot
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-alt: "Pre-cue parameter medians and 95 percent credible intervals: a and c on a 0 to 6 activation scale, f on a 0 to 1 scale, colored blue, orange, and green."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("data", "figures", "m3_complex_parameters.png"))
```

::: {.small}
Medians and 95% credible intervals. Filtering is shown on the 0–1 scale.
:::

::: {.notes}
This fit uses only pre-cue responses. a and c describe item activation and
context binding; f scales distractor activation relative to targets.
The same f scales distractor item and binding contributions in the standard
complex-span model. Interpret these estimates alongside the predictive check,
which shows systematic underprediction of other-distractor responses.
:::
